en: Record of the Essential Meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
Those who investigate the three vehicles through their gradual stages may fathom its boundaries;
yet those who seek the one vehicle in its perfect fusion cannot know its source or bottom. This is truly because the discourse that accords with the nature of reality exhausts all phenomena.
Pervading the ten directions throughout the realms,
this inexhaustible discourse encompasses the ocean of lands and includes the nine periods of time;
these layers manifest one within another, their origins and manifestations distinct yet interwoven.
They revolve and interrelate through the mutual reflection of principal and attendant aspects;
when rolled up, not a single word exists outside [this unity],
while the Śrāvakas conceal their sight and hearing within its expanse.
When unfolded, its numerical calculations are difficult to fathom;
Mañjuśrī looked upward and advanced his estimation to the subsequent position.
How could this be measured by ordinary sentiments, or conceived by those of shallow understanding?
However, having practiced listening and study for several years, my affection and delight have increased all the more.
Relying on the instructions of my teacher and possessing some limited insight and learning,
I have privately recorded these notes in chapters, titled the *Guanmai yi ji* (Record of the Meaning of the Channels).
Now, I shall briefly excerpt and analyze this sutra.
The contextual meaning throughout the text exhibits many different tendencies;
for now, I will clarify it by means of four such tendencies.
The remaining points should be understood by applying this same principle of reflection.
Regarding the "four powers":
the first is the power of mutual succession without end.
Second, the textual momentum of summarizing characteristics;
third, the textual momentum of unfolding without obstruction;
fourth, the textual momentum of taking up through question and answer.
Regarding the first point, the inexhaustibility of successive transmission, there are further two gates: first, one becoming many through successive unfolding;
second, many returning to one through successive convergence.
The second category establishes the fundamental nature.
Regarding the first point, "expanding the one into the many":
this refers to initially expanding and grasping the pure *dharmadhātu*.
There are two gates: that of principle (li) and that of wisdom (zhi).
These distinguish between bodhi and nirvāṇa. Furthermore, within the gate of principle, there is the distinction between essence (ti) and function (yong).
These are precisely the three characters "Great, Vaipulya" (Dafangguang) in the title.
Furthermore, the aspect of wisdom is divided into cause and fruit;
these are precisely the three characters "Buddha, Flower Ornament" (Fohuayan) in the title.
Thus, by means of the name as a whole, it is threaded together to achieve expression;
this is precisely the single character "sūtra" (經) within the title.
Nevertheless, when taken collectively from what precedes and what follows, there are seven characters in distinction.
This constitutes the title of the scripture as a single work.
Furthermore, this title may be expanded to form the First Assembly;
therein, the "five seas" and so forth represent the principle (*li*).
The ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and so forth are wisdom (*jñāna*).
The two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—are the fruit;
the adornment of the youth is the cause.
Now, both principle and wisdom, cause and effect, are manifested together; thus,
they unfold into a single assembly,
which constitutes, in its entirety, the Assembly of the Result as the Object of Faith.
Furthermore, this single assembly is further expanded into seven subsequent assemblies.
Within the preceding causal stage,
there are distinct divisions for faith, understanding, practice, vows, and realization, as well as differences in the manner of attaining faith and understanding.
These are considered six assemblies;
collectively, they constitute the causal assemblies for being able to have faith,
because in each individual assembly, the faith and understanding all possess a fruit that is the object of faith.
Therefore, including the preceding sections, there are seven assemblies in total.
This is because dharmas such as faith arise by depending on objects and do not originate from themselves;
furthermore, once these dharmas such as faith have reached fulfillment, one will necessarily realize and enter the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
There is an eighth [category], which constitutes the stage of realization and entry (*praveśa-samavasaraṇa*).
This is because it is only through the dharmas such as faith (*śraddhā*) that one realizes and enters the *dharmadhātu*, thereby reaching the ultimate.
As for the statement that faith and the others are separately opened up and distinguished from the stage of realization and entry (*samavasaraṇa*), [it is because...]
This extends from the end of the second assembly to the conclusion of the sixth assembly,
comprehensively clarifying the five stages beginning with faith;
these constitute the entirety of the cultivation of causal practices.
The seventh and eighth [stages] specifically clarify practice and realization;
that is, the profound resonance between principle and wisdom.
This is based on the differences in the stages of understanding, practice, realization, and progression.
Thus, it is divided in total into eight assemblies (*parivarta*).
Furthermore, within the section on realization (*pratyakṣa*),
it is further subdivided into fifty-five assemblies.
This refers to the first [section] of the eighth assembly,
beginning with Mañjuśrī and ending with Samantabhadra at the very end.
This is because it manifests the virtues of the dharma-realm by taking the persons who serve as its basis as evidence.
Thus, including both the preceding and subsequent sections, there are sixty-three assemblies in total;
for the stages of understanding, practice, and realization are simultaneous and devoid of temporal sequence.
Furthermore, each assembly of spiritual friends is expanded.
This is the inexhaustible, infinitely layered assembly;
it is like the Rishi grasping Sudhana’s hand and causing him to see assemblies as numerous as unspeakably unspeakable atoms of dust.
Furthermore, the text below states:
In the Land of Universal Gates, one beholds as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in a trichiliocosm;
these constitute the inexhaustible, infinitely nested assemblies.
This should be understood according to the text.
Since this is the case for one cognitive object (vijñeya) in such a layered manner,
the same principle applies to all others accordingly.
Furthermore, they further unfold unspeakably unspeakable assemblies,
pervading all worlds— whether of different or similar species, as numerous as atoms and hair-pores— where Bodhisattvas, with their primary and attendant retinues, are arrayed in infinite layers.
Because it universally integrates the fundamental and the derivative,
it constitutes an infinitely layered convergence.
This should be understood by reflecting upon the concluding and connecting passages of the sutra.
As for the formation of the second category of compendiums:
this involves expanding upon the aforementioned infinite, multi-layered assemblies.

It encompasses the ten directions and penetrates the three periods of time, exhausting all worlds—whether of similar or dissimilar types—as numerous as the atoms of dust. Within each and every one of these layers, the ten assemblies are fully present, and within each assembly, the ten teachings are expounded to manifest their inexhaustibility.
Thus, summarizing and condensing these various assemblies, they are designated as the "Lower Version," which consists of one hundred thousand verses.
Furthermore, this Lower Version is expanded upon.

Throughout all worlds of the same and different classes, extending to the ten directions, and throughout all worlds of the same and different classes pervading the entire Dharma-realm, reaching as far as the atoms within each world of the same and different classes—each and every one of these, layered upon another, possesses the tenfold teaching; the "ten" signifies inexhaustibility, and because of the layered interdependence of the principal and its attendants.
Summarizing and concluding this exposition,
it is designated as the "Middle-Length Version," consisting of four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses.
Furthermore, expanding upon this Middle-Length Version:

This is because it exhaustively encompasses all similar and dissimilar worlds throughout the ten directions, exhausting all such worlds—both similar and dissimilar—in their infinite layers; and because it explains, through the "Main Gate" (honmon), all these layered manifestations of the ten aspects, along with all their primary and attendant elements, in their infinite layers.
Furthermore, summarizing and condensing this teaching,
it constitutes the "Upper Version," which consists of as many verses as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms.
Expanding upon this Upper Version, [there is the Middle Version].

Because it exhaustively explains all successive layers of the ten directions; because it exhaustively explains all successive layers of the ten periods of time; because it exhaustively explains all successive layers of the ten worlds of similar and dissimilar types; because it exhaustively explains all successive layers of the ten subtle dust motes and hair-paths; because it exhaustively explains all successive layers within the Ten Principal Gates; because it exhaustively explains all successive layers within the principal gates and their retinues; and because it exhaustively explains all successive layers of internal equality.

This is the general summary that concludes this entire system: the tenfold manifestation of all things, each layer upon layer, is called the "Inexhaustible"; the tenfold manifestation of all things, layer upon layer, is called the "Extensive Text.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states:
Even if one were to use ink from the great oceans and pens as numerous as the heaps of Mount Sumeru,
one still could not exhaustively record the meaning and flavor of each chapter and even each individual phrase of this sutra.
As explained at length in the sutra:
if this is so for one chapter,
it is likewise so for the remaining chapters, as well as for the principal and attendant elements.
It is the same for all categories and their primary and secondary associates.
Since this is so for all categories and their primary and secondary associates,
it is likewise so for all other instances of the tenfold categories and their primary and secondary associates arranged in successive layers.
Since all things are thus layered with ten aspects and possess both principal and attendant elements,
so too does every single phrase, syllable, and flavor possess ten aspects and principal and attendant elements in a layered manner;
and since every single phrase, syllable, flavor, and their attendants are thus, [the same applies to all].
Thus, the locus of support is layered with tenfold aspects, and the principal and its associates are likewise layered;
this cannot be known in its full extent,
for it is beyond the capacity of speech or the brush to manifest.

This is the ultimate teaching on the infinite layers of the ten directions and ten methods, which pervade all without end; wherein every single atom of the dharma-realm, every hair-tip, and so forth, each possesses ten layers upon layers, along with their infinite primary and attendant elements, forming a totality of endless, successive strata.
According to this teaching, there are inexhaustible layers, each possessing the ten aspects, as well as the primary and attendant retinues; all these layers possess the ten aspects fundamentally.
This is known from the concluding text of the sutra.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"If one wishes to fully expound even a single phrase of the Dharma,
it could not be exhausted even in incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*)," and so forth.
Contemplate this according to the analogy of Indra’s net.
In summary, the Universal Eye possesses ten assemblies in a state of profound interpenetration.
In this manner, they unfold successively in infinite layers, each possessing tenfold teachings.
In the remaining sections of the Original Gate (*honmon*), each layer contains the ten gates of the Original Gate;
furthermore, within the Original Gate itself, each successive layer contains the ten gates.

Since the future and the past are both present therein, they all share the same substance or possess different substances while being mutually identical, mutually inclusive, and mutually encompassing; one should understand this by applying the principle that these layers simultaneously and repeatedly contain the ten gates.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Inexpressible eons may yet be fully described,
but the inexpressible cannot be exhausted."
That "the ocean of fruition is ineffable" is precisely this meaning;
it is the assembly where the ten Buddhas are perfectly interfused.
However, these successive explanations that reach the ultimate limit of infinity all flow from the most pure *dharmadhātu*;
they are precisely the differentiation within non-differentiation.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"There is nothing that does not flow from the Dharmakāya," and so forth;
one should contemplate this alone.
Thus far, this has been presented according to one perspective,
based on what can be compiled and what can be clearly explained.
In this way, there are yet many other perspectives and many other original versions.
Regarding what is currently being taught and what has been constantly taught, their limits cannot be fully manifested or known;
they should be understood by analogy with similar cases, as explained in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature" (Svabhāva-utpatti-parivarta). Reflect upon this.
Regarding the second section, "The Absence of Characteristics in Summary," there are further three gates.
The first is the summary of the extensive into the concise.
Second, the comprehensive inclusion through meaning;
third, the subsumption of the derivative into the fundamental.
First, regarding the subsumption of the extensive into the concise:

This is the comprehensive summary that presents the teachings on the eternal and the manifest as being immediate, inexhaustible, and layered, constituting the ultimate discourse endowed with the ten profundities.
Within these teachings on the eternal and the manifest, it employs concrete phenomena to reveal and elucidate the truth.
Know that the remainder is unspeakably unspeakable;
it cannot be recorded by brush or ink.
As the sutra says:
What I have expounded is like a single drop in the ocean. Furthermore,
this scroll contains inexhaustible, layered teachings that possess the tenfold perfect interfusion of the infinite and the boundless.
This is considered the expanded version because each and every phrase concludes by universally synthesizing the teachings,
being endowed with tenfold inexhaustibility within inexhaustibility, and being endowed with tenfold all-encompassing discourse.
Furthermore, the expanded version of the fascicles is designated as the "Superior Text" (shangben).

This is because every phrase and every sentence is interconnected and exhaustive, encompassing all categories of beings—both those of the same kind and those of different kinds—repeatedly endowed with the ten worlds and so forth, along with their primary and attendant retinues; everything is repeatedly endowed with the ten, leaving nothing unexhausted.
Furthermore, the first fascicle serves as the middle fascicle,

because after each assembly and each chapter, it universally pervades the entire dharma-realm— including the realms of atoms, paths, and the tips of hairs— wherein all things are layered and interpenetrating, fully endowed with the ten inexhaustible qualities, and universally connected.
Furthermore, the middle fascicle is so titled because it connects all the preceding assemblies through their manifold layers;
moreover, the lower fascicle constitutes a single assembly.
Nevertheless, because each assembly is complete in every respect,
that which is called "complete" is as follows:
All [versions] state ten [chapters],
signifying inexhaustibility.
Furthermore, they are collectively compiled into one assembly.
The two gates of "person" (pudgala) and "dharma" correspond to the sequence of first [discussing] the dharma and subsequently the person.
Furthermore, the fascicle represents the perfect realization of mind and objects.
This refers to the sequence from the Assembly of Mañjuśrī up to the Assembly of Samantabhadra.
Furthermore, it consists of seven characters because the sūtra title fully encompasses both the expressive words and the expressed meaning, as well as the wisdom and its object, and cause and effect.
As previously explained.
Furthermore, the seventh fascicle is divided into three parts,
and likewise, the third fascicle is divided into two parts.
It is both that the second fascicle constitutes one [whole] and that the first fascicle is not one;
it is also because the nature contains ten thousand virtues, such that there is no phenomenon to which it does not pervade.
Second, regarding the comprehensive inclusion through the meaning:
following the flow of the text and the terminology of the meaning,
it is clearly explained that throughout this entire treatise there are, in total, four characters.
It is also complete in both words and meaning. What are the four?
First, the teaching.
This means that although the text is vast and extensive,
it is all subsumed within the single character of "teaching" (jiao),
which is precisely the character "sūtra" (jing) in the title.
There are two meanings.
Although the categories of meaning are infinite,
they are all subsumed within the single meaning of dependent origination.
This refers precisely to the "Vaipulya" (Extensive) section within the title.
The third part consists of three aspects:
namely, the practice of understanding, cause and effect, and virtuous functions.
Although each is established differently,
according to their mode of establishment,
they are all subsumed within the single category of "that which is produced" (*pariniṣpanna*).
This refers precisely to the "Buddha," "Flower Adornment" (*Avataṃsaka*), and so forth mentioned in the title.
Regarding the four locations:
these refer to all the infinitely layered assemblies of both similar and dissimilar types that occur in infinite succession.
The "single locus" refers to the eye;
it is precisely the basis upon which the assembly relies.
Now, speaking in terms of the general summary:
However, the meaning is of a single nature;
the teaching is of a single text;
and the realization is of a single thought-moment.
The locus is a single object. Why? Because one is all.
Because all is one.
As the Sūtra says:
"To know one is to know many; to know many is to know one."
"The meaning and flavor are pure and fully perfected," and so forth;
it further says:
"Within one, understand the immeasurable."
Because among the immeasurable [teachings], they are understood as being one and the same.
Master Tong said:
"A single word leaves nothing unsummarized."
This refers to what is called "the extraordinary teaching that is ultimately no different from the full [reality].
Third, regarding "subsuming the branches and returning to the root":
Now, examining the preceding title:
thus, the single character "Great" (Dà) is the general name for this entire treatise,
referring to the ocean of fruition that is investigated.
The two characters "Vaipulya" (Broad and Extensive) signify the capacity for the ocean-like qualities of the fruit;
they comprehensively clarify the causal and functional operation of the entire section.
The single character "Buddha" signifies the wisdom that realizes [this].
The person capable of expounding the single section on Penetrating Clarity (tōmyō) has perfected both understanding and practice regarding the causes of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Furthermore, by subsuming function back into essence, it is solely principle (*li*).
To subsume causes within results belongs solely to the Buddha.
Furthermore, since it is through the Dharma that one becomes a person,
and since persons have no self-nature, this is the true lineage.
If nature lacks intrinsic nature, then it is not nature.
To explain this meaning in its entirety constitutes the teaching;
yet the teaching is itself no teaching.
Why is this? Because the nature of syllables is free from [inherent existence], which is itself liberation;
and because the ocean of fruition transcends speech and is ineffable.
This is both differentiation and non-differentiation.
The Treatise states:
"There is no realization of this Dharmakāya that is not [the fruit of] Non-returning."
This is what is meant by that.
Regarding the third point, "unimpeded in both unfolding and rolling up," one first clarifies unfolding and subsequently clarifies rolling up.
Regarding the first unfolding:
when opening it, different materials are employed,
and thus their applications vary.
The distinctions in the nature of conditions and the diversity of dharma-gates are precisely what is meant by "Mahāvaipulya."
Since causes differ from their effects,
the practices of understanding vary; thus,
there are distinctions in their realizations.
The master and disciple differ;
they are precisely the Buddha and the *Avataṃsaka*.
This is because there are differences in how the sutra is stitched together and explained.
This refers to the teaching that all things are inexhaustible and possess tenfold layers;
it is explained extensively as previously analyzed,
and should be understood accordingly.
As for the two fascicles,
there are further five gates.
The first is the comprehensive categorization by means of stages.
Second, the subsumption and convergence according to persons;
third, clarifying the Dharma by means of persons;
fourth, the perfect interfusion of objects and wisdom.
The five [stages] merge equally into the ocean of fruition.
Regarding the first [stage], which subsumes all positions:
although the text of this sutra is indeed inexhaustible, [it is summarized as follows].
In total, these are subsumed under three sections:
namely, understanding (*adhimukti*), practice (*pratipatti*), and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Within the section on understanding:
It is divided internally into two sections.
First, within the first assembly, the Buddha’s two fruits—the primary (the Dharma-body) and the secondary (the form-body)—are presented to encourage the arising of faith and joy;
thus, according to this text, this is termed the "Section on Presenting the Fruits to Encourage Practice and Generate Faith."
Second, the explanation:
from the second assembly through the sixth assembly,
it extensively clarifies the characteristics of how understanding arises sequentially throughout the five stages.
Thus, according to this text, this is titled "The Section on Cultivating the Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generate Understanding.
Second.
In the seventh assembly, it further clarifies the cultivation that accomplishes the practices of the preceding five stages.
One immediately integrates the various understandings previously discussed to establish one's practice;
thus, according to this text, it is titled "The Section on Entrusting Oneself to the Dharma to Advance in Cultivating Practice.
How is this known?
The "reconvening at Universal Radiance" (Pūrvābhāsa) refers precisely to this event. If it were not so,
why would there not have been a reconvening during the first or third assemblies?
Since the second assembly was the beginning of the exposition on faith and understanding (*adhimukti*),
and now that understanding has been realized and put into practice,
it is logically necessary for faith to serve as the primary guide.
Therefore, the purpose of this "Reunion at Universal Radiance" (Puguang) lies herein.

It may also manifest that all the assemblies occurred simultaneously, such that on the second week of the second seven-day period, the teaching was proclaimed all at once and universally, without any sequence or distinction of before and after.
Why is this? Because both the single mention and the repeated mention are identical to the second seven-day period.
Three.
In the eighth and first assembly, it is further explained that one enters the Dharma by relying on persons and realizes the fruits previously mentioned;
thus, according to this text, this section is titled "The Section on Entering Realization and Accomplishing Virtue by Relying on Persons."
How is this known?
It is because those who realize the fruits previously mentioned initially aspired to and delighted in those very fruits.
By generating faith and understanding,
once that understanding has been realized and put into practice,
one immediately realizes the aforementioned fruit.
Therefore, this assembly is indeed the previous assembly.
Were it not so, one could not give rise to faith and understanding by citing the former as the cause for the latter result.
Since understanding has already been integrated into practice,
how could there be a separate realization?
Now, this is established based on the mutual generation of the textual meaning and its logical sequence.
Thus, one knows that the later assembly is identical to the earlier assembly.
For this reason, they are collectively divided into three sections,
which most closely accords with the text of the sūtra.
What has been explained above can be understood through reflection.
Second, regarding the synthesis according to the persons:
these are subsequently subsumed to form a single assembly.
It refers exclusively to the first assembly. Why?
Because the first assembly is the objective basis upon which the preceding explanations and so forth depend.
Upon reaching the subsequent resolution and fulfillment, one immediately realizes the distinctions previously mentioned,
forming a single, perfectly integrated practice and virtue,
thereby attaining entry into the aforementioned Dharma.
Ultimately, words fail.
Therefore, the eighth stage entrusts the person to clearly demonstrate the entry into the Dharma-realm;
such is the underlying intention.
Regarding the term "clarifying those who rely on others":
this refers to the eighth assembly, in which the Tathāgata himself entered the Lion’s Vigorous Display Samādhi,
causing all the bodhisattvas to enter the dharma-realm.
The fruits previously cited are intended to encourage joy;
this corresponds to the first assembly.
It is because the Tathāgata himself entered the *vaiśāradya-samādhi* (the samādhi of heroic prowess) desiring that all bodhisattvas should likewise realize and enter it.
Furthermore, from Mañjuśrī at the beginning to Gopī at the end,
these represent the signs of generating understanding through the convergence of prior cultivation of causes with the realization of the fruit;
they correspond precisely to the first five assemblies.
Because Sudhana inquired of various people to seek distinct faiths and understandings for the sake of extensive and universal knowledge.
From Māyā onwards to the final Mañjuśrī,
this represents the prior entrustment to the Dharma, the progressive cultivation, and the perfection of practice;
it corresponds to the seventh assembly.
Since the practice in the seventh assembly has been completed,
Mañjuśrī subsequently bestows a necklace upon him to manifest the perfection of correct conduct and to cause him to cultivate merit.
Māyā is the mother of all Buddhas;
she is placed first because her perfected practice is able to give birth to the Buddhas.
Samantabhadra is situated at the rear.
When the Dharma-realm of dependent origination is taken as the object of focus,
it serves to manifest the realization and entry into the perfection of practice;
this corresponds to the eighth assembly.
By seeing Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, one sees as many spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) as there are atoms.
Third, regarding the inclusion of persons according to their status:
this refers to those within the assembly of spiritual friends.
Furthermore, beginning with Mañjuśrī and ending with Gopā,
there are forty-one individuals in total;
these are termed the "characteristics of practice through the stages of entrustment."
The five stages, beginning with "Entrusting the Previous Letter," involve seeking understanding based on the person and practicing the path progressively.
The second [section], beginning from Māyā and continuing through Śrīgarbha-kumāra and others,
comprises eleven individuals in total;
this is titled "Entering the True Aspect by Conjoining Conditions."
This refers to the realization of the Dharma-realm through the practice of the five preceding stages.
The third stage, that of Maitreya alone,
is termed the "characteristic of the cause for the integration of virtues."
This immediately subsumes the virtues of the preceding practices as the primary cause for entering realization;
because this differs from the "establishment of proof" mentioned previously, two distinct positions are opened.
The fourth section consists of the single figure of Mañjuśrī at the end.
This is called the wisdom that illuminates the non-dual aspect.
Thus, as practice reaches its ultimate fulfillment, clear awakening resides within one’s breast;
this illumination of prior understanding and practice is the single, true, great wisdom.
Furthermore, there is no distinction between before and after, clarity and obscurity, and so forth.
The fifth is the single figure Samantabhadra,
whose name signifies the vast characteristics of manifesting the cause.
This means that initial awakening (śikṣā-bodha) is identical to great wisdom (mahājñāna), manifesting before one and pervading the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) without limit,
universally encompassing and entering into it.
Fourth, regarding the perfect fusion of object and wisdom:
Furthermore, among the aforementioned persons,
they are collectively subsumed into two categories:
Mañjuśrī is the great wisdom that realizes, and...
This refers to the aforementioned practices of understanding and application (*adhimukti-caryā*) and so forth.
Second, Samantabhadra is the Dharma-realm that is realized;
this is precisely what was previously described as that which is believed in and entered.
Why is this? It is because Mañjuśrī corresponds to the stage of Prajñāpāramitā,
while Samantabhadra corresponds to the gateway of the Dharmadhātu.
As for why this is so, the Master said:
"The Tripitaka Master stated that there is a sutra which speaks in this manner."
Furthermore, upon examining the meaning and the flow of the text within this sutra, it is clear that such an intention is deeply embedded therein.
Moreover, since the ancient masters have already determined that the later Mañjuśrī is named for the non-dual aspect of wisdom and illumination.
Therefore, we know that all the people mentioned previously were in fact the single person, Mañjuśrī, who appears later.
Thus, the subsequent text states:
"Sudhana returned and passed through one hundred and ten cities before arriving once again at Mañjuśrī."
This is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, the text states:
"Mañjuśrī taught me methods such as divination and calculation."
Furthermore, the Elder said:
"By the power of Mañjuśrī’s recollection," and so forth.
Moreover, the later passage says:
"Good son Mañjuśrī, he is your spiritual friend.
He is able to cause you to be born into the family of the Tathāgata,
to nurture your roots of goodness, and to accumulate a mass of merit."

Up to the fulfillment of great vows and the purification of all dharma-gates, all of which arise from the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī; once wisdom is perfected, one realizes the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, because [the stage of] Fulfillment follows [the stage of] Samantabhadra,
the subsequent text states:
"I manifest the realm of the Buddha within each and every pore; observe this with careful attention," and so forth.
It further says:
"You should first observe my pure Dharma-body," and so forth.
The commentary states:
Since it instructs one to contemplate the pure *dharmakāya*,
we know that Sudhana beheld Samantabhadra.
This is precisely the realization of the dharma-dhātu.
Furthermore, they are unified as one;
that is to say, the object and wisdom are in profound accord, without any distinction.
Therefore, in the subsequent [section], Mañjuśrī no longer has a physical form. Why is this so?
Because the initial vision of Mañjuśrī marks the very beginning of Sudhana’s faith.
The passage from "afterwards not seen" marks the conclusion of Sudhana’s fulfillment of wisdom;
all individuals encountered in the interim represent the successive stages of Sudhana’s spiritual practice.
Because Sudhana’s obstructions were exhausted and his delusions eliminated, he never for a moment stirred a thought.
Therefore, the reflective illumination is nothing other than the initial mind; there is no difference.
That one does not see anything afterwards is due to the presence of conceptual thought.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
"Arising from the wisdom of Mañjuśrī," and so forth.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"Initial awakening is identical to original awakening."
There is no distinction between non-enlightenment and enlightenment;
this is what is meant by that.
Fifth, "merging equally into the ocean of fruition" refers to this.
This means that because the causal practice has reached perfection, one sinks into the ocean of fruition;
free from beginning and end, fully endowed with virtue,
it transcends words and cuts off discursive thought, being realized only through direct correspondence.
In this way, the rolling up and unfolding are unimpeded and simultaneous, following the discourse as its gateway;
ultimately, there is no sequence of before or after.
Therefore, because the rolling up and unfolding possess such unimpediment, they are difficult to describe in detail.
One should contemplate this according to the text.
Thus, the Sūtra says:
"Such a true son of the Buddha."
When sentient beings desire to deliberate upon the profound and subtle meaning,
their minds become confused and they go mad.
This is what is meant by that.
Regarding the fourth question-and-answer, which takes up the text, there are also two parts:
first, the question-and-answer that reconciles contradictions.
Second, the exhortation to practice and study.
First, regarding the resolution of contradictions through question and answer:
the question asks, "Since it was previously stated that this is the Māyā Assembly..."
If the preceding conditions constitute its reality, how can there still be ten different people after they have gathered?
Answer: As for there being ten people after they have gathered:
This reveals the true excellence of dependent origination;
it relies upon ten aspects to manifest its inexhaustibility. Why is this so?
Because they do not depart from Māyā,
these are all the actual virtues of Māyā; that is to say,
by relying on the preceding five stages, one practices together with the three worlds until reaching the ultimate.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"I am the mother of all Buddhas;
all Buddhas are born from me," and so forth.
This may also signify that each stage is itself a state of mutual fusion and integration, where contraction and expansion are without obstruction.
Therefore, the meaning behind the statement that "each and every stage realizes Buddhahood" resides precisely in this.
Question: Māyā has no substantial body;
it is merely the convergence of the preceding stages that constitutes the body.
It is the same for other persons as well.
Why is it that not all [beings] possess these ten?
The answer is: those who possess these ten persons within Māyā herself are precisely those in whom each of the aforementioned ten persons is fully present.
Why is this? Because Māyā immediately merged with all the people previously mentioned,
becoming a single body with them.
Since each and every individual is Māyā,
and Māyā is each and every individual,
that which is now fully present within Māyā alone [is so].
This is the intended meaning.
When it is asked whether Māyā is the same as the aforementioned individuals,
and it is replied that she possesses [these qualities] while others also possess them, [the point is as follows].
One might also argue that these various people are themselves the later Māyā;
why then is she complete in the former [life] but incomplete in the latter?
The answer is: Māyā is the general [designation].
The others are specific [factors].
It is sufficient that the general [condition] be present for the specific ones to be present. Why is this?
The individual is not yet ultimate;
it is the collective that is ultimate.
If it is not yet ultimate...
There is nothing else to be distinguished;
how, then, could it be "complete"?
Therefore, that which is complete within Māyā—
This is also possessed by other people.

Question: Among the eight assemblies, why is it that in the four assemblies concerning ascending to heaven, it is stated in all cases that [the Buddha] does not rise from the Bodhi tree or from his own assembly, but ascends to other realms?
Why is it that regarding the three assemblies among humans, it is not said that they do not arise from here but ascend to there?
The answer is that there are two meanings.
The first is based on understanding (*adhigama*).
Second, regarding practice (*caryā*).
Within the first explanation, there are again three parts:
first, the proximate; second, the remote; and third, the general.
Regarding the first "proximate" [realm]:
because the three locations among humans are likewise within the human realm,
they share no difference in terms of their physical basis.
That they are naturally encompassed by one another goes without saying;
this is why it is not stated that one does not arise here before ascending there.
Second, regarding the two types of distance:
Because the categories of humans and devas are vastly separated and differ from one another, it is difficult to perceive how they mutually encompass one another;
therefore, the preceding is brought forward to clarify what follows.
This is precisely the unimpeded nature of dependent origination, wherein all assemblies occur simultaneously.
Regarding the three generalities:
by means of the general, the particular is subsumed;
the particular exists within the general.
The ascent and descent differ;
yet all are said not to depart from the Bodhi tree.
While they are thus, there are inherent distinctions within the gate of mutual fusion and pervasion.
Although it has departed from that [place], it is always here;
this is for the purpose of producing understanding in sentient beings.
It is said that one does not depart from this place to ascend to that other.
Second, regarding the practitioner, there are again two parts:
first, the exposition of the meaning.
Second, the explanation of the defense.
Regarding the first:
however, assemblies such as those for ascending to heaven are spoken of in terms of the place where one relies upon liberation.
Since understanding is complete, one immediately proceeds to realize it without deviation;
therefore, the latter two [stages] are not discussed.
Furthermore, they are not analogous to the heavens.
Such is the intention.
Second, because faith itself does not possess a fixed position,
these two stages are not mentioned.
Question: It was stated above that when Sudhana arrives, Mañjuśrī immediately says, "Wisdom is fulfilled and reflects back;
this is solely the initial mind, with nothing else. How is this so?
Why does the sutra clarify that Sudhana traverses various stages?
The answer is: there are two kinds of traversing through the stages.
First, in terms of the teaching’s sequential progression (*panthāna*).
Therefore, there are successive stages and levels that differ in their gradations;
it is in reference to this that Sudhana’s progression through these stages is discussed.
Second, regarding the meaning:
because the great dharma-realm of dependent origination is simultaneously complete and devoid of sequence, position, or priority and posteriority,
it is according to this that Sudhana’s single lifetime is described.
Now, these two meanings are examined together.
Nevertheless, the successive stages do not depart from the initial mind;
a single lifetime does not shift into many kalpas.
What is elucidated in the sutra is fully consistent with this meaning.
Thus, the sutra says:
"A single thought-moment is immeasurable eons."
That immeasurable eons are equal to a single thought-moment:
if we now speak in terms of subsuming the meaning through the teaching,
this is called the "Identity Teaching of the One Vehicle."
If one speaks in terms of subsuming the teachings according to their meaning,
this is called the Separate Teaching One Vehicle. Nevertheless,
although Sudhana traverses the stages, he does not depart from his original resolve.
This is based on that teaching.
Question: For what reason is there no further indication of a future destination or a concluding summary for Mañjuśrī at the very end?
Answer: Because Mañjuśrī’s causal practice has already reached its ultimate consummation.
Pointing toward the subsequent stage is precisely the realization of interpenetration.
Seeing the one as being all, the principle is perfected;
therefore, there is no further need for a concluding summary.
Therefore, a sutra says:
"Within the marks, signs, limbs, joints, and every pore of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva,
Sudhana beheld unspeakably unspeakable oceans of worlds filled with Buddhas."
Each and every Tathāgata has an entourage consisting of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of great bodhisattvas, and so forth.
This is the second section, which exhorts students to practice.
The above is a brief summary of the introductory portion of the sutra.
It is like peering at the heavens through a tube;
its remaining manifestations are manifold,
and one cannot know their limits.
Throughout all future kalpas,
I vow to complete my practice;
may I only wish that in every successive body I receive, I shall always be born within this assembly.
Just as Sudhana thought in his mind:
"At the end of the kalpa, fire shall arise in all worlds,
burning everything down through the six heavens until they are utterly consumed."
One must enter this conflagration of the kalpa to seek the Dharma;
with a mind of true resolve in the armor of one's vow,
those who have faith and take refuge in its cultivation will swiftly realize Bodhi.
Whatever you have seen or heard according to your capacity will surely become a firm seed;
you ought to give rise to great joy and rejoice at having encountered this rare opportunity.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Sudhana, you should give rise to great joy;
before long, you shall attain the great fruit of retribution."
Therefore, what the Bodhisattvas cultivated over immeasurable kalpas,
you have now fully attained in a single lifetime.
Even those who wish to obtain such a Dharma as this [shall do so].
"One should practice as Sudhana did," and so forth;
it further states:
"The Buddhas of the past exclusively sought bodhi and cultivated this practice."
Throughout immeasurable kalpas within all conditioned phenomena, one has undergone immeasurable suffering, yet still has not encountered [it]. ...
up to the point where it says:
They shall obtain great and wholesome benefits,
fulfill their great vows,
and draw near to all Buddhas.
"Being a true son of the Buddha,
one will certainly become a guide for others to Buddhahood," and so forth.
